title: Causal forecasting and prevention of systemic financial cascades

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an operational way to forecast when losses at individual financial institutions could spread into a system-wide cascade, and to predict which interventions would interrupt that spread. It would connect a forecast of what might happen with a causal explanation of how losses travel and how particular actions would change the outcome. The capability is hypothetical; the supplied evidence establishes a relevant theoretical mechanism, not achievement of this broader objective.

Proposed scope: the causal account would link contractual exposures, overlapping asset holdings, funding conditions, forced asset sales and changing expectations. It would need to remain useful as institutions adjust their behavior and as interventions alter the system being forecast. The supplied abstract motivates the interbank-liability component. The other channels, incomplete exposure information and changing networks are retained as research objectives and proposed challenges; their importance and treatment are not established by the supplied source.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability could make financial stability substantially more preventive. Decision-makers could use estimates of propagation risk and intervention effects to decide where to reduce exposures, provide liquidity or interrupt a developing cascade. The supplied theoretical result gives this objective a concrete motivation: denser financial connections can improve resilience to sufficiently small shocks while helping larger shocks spread. A useful operational method would therefore have to assess circumstances and shock size, rather than treat greater interconnectedness as uniformly protective or dangerous.

Conditional synthesis: the direct advance would be better decisions about exposures, liquidity and interventions under uncertainty. If those decisions reliably reduced systemic damage, downstream possibilities could include fewer disruptions to credit and less spillover into investment and employment. Neither the size of these benefits nor their attainability is established by the supplied material. Predicting and limiting financial propagation would not guarantee prevention of every crisis or recession, whose causes and consequences extend beyond the mechanisms covered here.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this proposal is the combination of prospective cascade forecasting with credible predictions of intervention effects. A mechanism explaining how shocks can propagate is an essential ingredient, but does not by itself establish that an operational system can identify an approaching cascade, estimate its severity or select an action that improves the outcome. The retained abstract documents a theoretical interbank-network mechanism; it does not establish this combined capability or settle its present-day feasibility.

Proposed scientific and engineering barriers include reconstructing consequential exposures from incomplete information, combining distinct transmission channels without counting the same losses twice, and updating the network as funding and trading relationships change under stress. The model would also need to distinguish direct contractual losses from effects transmitted through asset prices, funding pressure and expectations. These are requirements implied by the intended scope, rather than difficulties independently documented by the supplied abstract.

Methodological synthesis: intervention prediction presents an additional causal problem. Institutions may respond to a forecast or policy action, changing the behavior on which the original prediction depended. Moreover, observing that losses subsided after an intervention would not alone show that the intervention caused the improvement. A convincing capability would need a defensible comparison with what would otherwise have happened, uncertainty estimates that reflect missing information, and evidence that its predictions remain useful as institutions adapt.

current_state.text: In their February 2015 paper, Systemic Risk and Stability in Financial Networks, Daron Acemoglu, Asuman Ozdaglar and Alireza Tahbaz-Salehi report a theoretical result about interbank-liability networks. Denser connections enhance financial stability for sufficiently small negative shocks, but beyond a shock-size threshold the same network features can facilitate propagation and greater fragility. This establishes a model-based distinction between resilience to small shocks and vulnerability to larger ones; it is not an empirical estimate of a universal crisis threshold.

The supplied review retained and assessed the article's landing page and abstract, rather than the linked full article. That material supports the dated theoretical mechanism but supplies no prospective forecasting results or validation of intervention choices. This is a limit on the available evidence, not a finding that the uninspected full paper contains no further analysis. The retained HTML was reported as untruncated, with no extraction issues; those properties do not make it a full-text record.

Evidence limitation: no freshness evidence was supplied to assess subsequent progress through November 1, 2026. The source artifact's November 11, 2026 retrieval date does not establish that later research was surveyed. The available inputs therefore support a description of the 2015 theoretical contribution, but do not establish the present frontier, achievable forecasting accuracy, demonstrated economic benefits or whether the entire proposed capability remains open today. No numerical forecasting performance or operational deployment results were supplied.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: publish prospective probabilistic forecasts across multiple financial systems and stress conditions, with forecast horizons and cascade outcomes defined before evaluation. Report calibration, false-alarm rates and missed-cascade rates, along with the predicted extent of damage and uncertainty. Evaluate forecasts on independent data against plausible alternatives. The protocol should specify what counts as a cascade and how systemic damage is measured; these are proposed evaluation requirements, not standards established by the supplied paper.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective cascade forecasts evaluated independently across multiple financial systems

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal demonstration: make intervention-specific predictions and use credible intervention evidence or natural experiments to test whether recommended actions reduce systemic damage relative to plausible alternatives. The evaluation should distinguish accurate risk prediction from evidence that acting on a recommendation improves outcomes. It should also state how it handles the fact that interventions are often chosen precisely where risks are greatest, which can make simple comparisons misleading.
completion_criteria.label: Causal evidence validates intervention-specific predictions of reduced systemic damage

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent evaluators should be able to reproduce the analysis using documented data definitions, model versions, assumptions and evaluation procedures, with controlled access where financial data cannot be made public. Demonstrations should identify required exposure coverage, sensitivity to missing information, update speed and performance when institutions change behavior. Success across a finite set of systems would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality or a guarantee against future crises. No numerical acceptance thresholds have been established in the supplied material.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction of analyses with documented practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: FIN-08, A causal theory linking trading activity to market-wide liquidity crashes, has the closest stated overlap. It focuses on propagation from trading and funding conditions into market-wide liquidity failure. FIN-02 has a broader proposed scope spanning institutional exposures and multiple transmission channels, with an explicit objective of forecasting cascades and evaluating interventions. A successful FIN-08 theory could inform part of FIN-02, while remaining a distinct innovation.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-03, Run-resistant financing of long-lived, illiquid investment, concerns financing arrangements that resist runs. Such arrangements could be among the mechanisms evaluated for cascade prevention, but designing resilient financing differs from forecasting propagation across a financial system. FIN-01, A general, testable theory of asset prices under adaptive behavior, overlaps through price changes and adaptation; its central target is asset-price explanation rather than systemic cascade prevention.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-09, Causal measurement of investment’s financial and real-world impact, shares the need to distinguish causal effects from observed associations, although its object is investment impact rather than crisis interventions. FIN-11, Operational limits on the financial value of information and arbitrage, could inform questions about the usefulness of financial forecasts and responses to information. It does not itself supply a causal model of systemic contagion.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-04, Low-cost, reliable insurance for previously uninsurable livelihoods; FIN-05, Scalable financing for creditworthy people and firms without conventional credit histories; and FIN-10, Scalable financing mechanisms for pure public goods, address different financing and risk-sharing objectives. Their arrangements could be examined for exposure to systemic stress, but their success would not establish the forecasting and prevention capability proposed here. FIN-06, Universally accessible, near-instant cross-border money transfer, and FIN-07, Cash-like privacy and resilience for digital money, concern payment and monetary infrastructure. Their resilience goals are relevant context, while remaining distinct from explaining and preventing system-wide financial cascades.

unresolved_issues: The supplied material does not establish subsequent progress through November 1, 2026 or whether the full proposed capability remains open today.
The linked full article was not retained for review; its additional methods, assumptions and results cannot be assessed from these inputs.
The roles and empirical importance of common holdings, funding, forced sales, expectations, incomplete exposures and changing networks require evidence beyond the supplied abstract.
Forecast horizons, cascade definitions, systemic-damage measures, comparator interventions and numerical acceptance thresholds remain unspecified.
Achievable forecast accuracy, credible identification of intervention benefits and the magnitude of economic gains remain undetermined.
Practical requirements for data coverage, confidential-data access, update speed and robustness to institutional adaptation remain to be established.

brief.title: Predicting and stopping the spread of financial losses
possible: When a bank runs into trouble, financial authorities could forecast whether its losses will spread into a chain reaction across the financial system. They could also predict which actions would interrupt that spread, with an explanation of how each action would help.
why: Authorities could use those forecasts to decide where to reduce financial commitments or provide cash before trouble spreads. More reliable prevention could mean fewer disruptions to lending, with less damage reaching investment and jobs.

sources.who: Daron Acemoglu, Asuman Ozdaglar and Alireza Tahbaz-Salehi
sources.showed: Their theoretical model showed that more connections through debts between banks can absorb small shocks but spread larger ones.
sources.quote:
However, beyond a certain point, dense interconnections serve as a
mechanism for the propagation of shocks, leading to a more fragile
financial system.
sources.cited_for: The same financial connections can help contain losses or help them spread, depending on the size of the shock.
sources.not_established: The model does not establish a real-world threshold for crises or demonstrate forecasts and effective interventions.

sources.who: Johannes Beutel, Sophia List and Gregor von Schweinitz
sources.showed: In historical banking-crisis tests, a conventional statistical model beat the machine learning methods tested when predicting periods beyond the data used to fit it.
sources.quote:
In line with economic intuition, these models identify credit expansions, asset price
booms and external imbalances as key predictors of systemic banking crises.
sources.cited_for: Forecasts need testing on outcomes beyond the data used to build the model.
sources.not_established: Predicting banking crises does not establish how losses will spread or which intervention will reduce the damage.

sources.showed: Their historical study found that Pennsylvania banks more exposed to New York shifted toward more liquid assets, which are easier to turn into cash. The authors concluded that bailouts likely contained a wider panic.
sources.quote:
Over the long-term though, only the lower 
correspondent deposits effect persisted.
sources.cited_for: Historical bank connections help reveal how distress spreads and how bailouts may contain it.
sources.not_established: This historical case does not validate advance predictions of which interventions would work across financial systems.

sources.who: Kartik Anand, Iman van Lelyveld and collaborators
sources.showed: They compared methods for reconstructing financial connections from incomplete data across markets. The best method depended on which features of the connections it needed to reproduce.
sources.quote:
We ﬁnd that the winner of the horse race depends on the feature
of the network that we seek to preserve during the reconstruction.
sources.cited_for: Missing financial connections can be estimated and tested, including while keeping underlying data confidential.
sources.not_established: Reconstructing connections does not establish accurate forecasts of spreading losses or effective intervention choices.

sources.who: Ilias Aarab, Thomas Gottron, Andrea Colombo, Jörg Reddig and Annalaura Ianiro
sources.showed: In a preprint, they combined detailed euro-area banking data into a network that separates different financial relationships. Combining those relationships into a single map could obscure which banks matter most in particular markets.
sources.quote:
We document pronounced cross-layer heterogeneity in connectivity and cen-
trality, and show that an aggregated (flattened) representation can mask economically relevant structure
and misidentify the institutions that are systemically important in specific markets.
sources.cited_for: Real banking data can connect several routes through which losses spread while preserving their differences.
sources.not_established: The network and model applications do not establish reliable advance forecasts or causal benefits from recommended interventions.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated separate parts of the capability. Acemoglu and colleagues explained theoretically why bank connections can contain small shocks yet amplify larger ones. Beutel and colleagues tested banking-crisis warnings against later historical outcomes.

Anand and colleagues compared ways to fill gaps in financial maps. Aarab and colleagues built a map that separates several kinds of banking relationships, in a preprint. Bluedorn and Park found historical evidence that bailouts likely contained a wider panic. These results do not establish the combined forecasting and prevention capability.
missing: Forecasts made before events unfold must reliably predict whether losses will spread and how much damage they will cause.
Tests must establish whether acting on a specific recommendation causes less damage than plausible alternatives.
Models must combine debts, shared investments, funding pressures, forced sales and expectations without counting losses twice.
Independent teams must reproduce results and establish how missing data and changing bank behavior affect performance.

milestones.label: Independently tested forecasts across financial systems
milestones.explanation: Advance forecasts would need independent tests across systems and stresses, with timing and outcomes defined beforehand and errors, damage and uncertainty assessed. This would establish whether warnings work beyond model-building data.

milestones.label: Evidence that predicted interventions reduce damage
milestones.explanation: Credible comparisons would have to show that specific actions reduce damage as predicted, accounting for why those actions were chosen. This would distinguish useful warnings from recommendations that actually improve outcomes.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction with practical limits established
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would need to reproduce analyses using documented data and methods, with confidential access where needed. Tests would establish limits from missing data, update speed and changing bank behavior.

uncertain: What should count as a spreading financial cascade, how far ahead should forecasts reach, and what performance would be good enough?
How accurately can models predict intervention benefits when banks change their behavior in response to warnings or policy?
How much could successful prevention reduce disruptions to lending, investment and employment?

page.title: Systemic risk forecasting and contagion prevention
page.definition: A system forecasts whether losses at financial institutions will propagate into a cascade and predicts which intervention will reduce system-wide losses. A cascade is a chain of losses amplified through financial exposures, funding withdrawals or forced asset sales.

goal.need: Laeven and Valencia identify 151 systemic banking-crisis episodes worldwide during 1970–2017. The table reports public outlays associated with stabilising banking systems. These costs motivate forecasting and intervention analysis; they do not measure the share caused by contagion or the amount this capability could prevent.

figures.caption: Median gross fiscal costs of banking crises in the 1970–2017 database
figures.note: Annual intervention outlays are divided by that year's nominal GDP and summed, before subtracting recoveries. Medians use available fiscal-cost observations within the 151-episode database; income-group observation counts were not located.

completion.title: Forecast-guided intervention causally reduces the losses from a financial cascade.
completion.criterion: For a specified financial network and horizon, a model forecasts cascade incidence and system-wide loss and ranks a named intervention against an alternative before action. A prospective evaluation establishes better forecasting performance than a specified benchmark under the authority's decision-loss function, and identifies a causal reduction in system-wide losses, including intervention costs, under the model-guided action, confirming the predicted ranking. Outcomes, comparator, horizon and loss function are fixed before evaluation. This is a minimal demonstration for the evaluated setting; no numerical acceptance standard was located.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside acceptance test for the combined capability was located.
completion.basis: Searches of BCBS stress-testing principles, OFR's research agenda, the Bank of England's SWES and 2025 analytical review, and cascade-forecast benchmarks, prizes and prospective protocols found no joint acceptance test. The SWES is explicitly “not a forecast”. The fallback requires the missing combination: prospective predictive skill and a causally supported benefit from acting on the prediction.

milestones.title: A financial-network model propagates institution-level losses into further institutional losses.
milestones.criterion: A mechanistic model transmits initial institution-level losses through financial connections into further losses. Acemoglu et al. established shock-dependent contagion theoretically in 2015. Anand et al. compared exposure-network reconstructions across 25 markets in 13 jurisdictions in 2018. Aarab et al. integrate five exposure layers using a list of 114 banking groups dated 1 June 2021; the journal version was published on 11 February 2026. These establish mechanisms and empirical inputs, without prospective cascade validation.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of the OFR and Bank of England research agendas located no common acceptance criterion for a mechanistic demonstration.

milestones.title: A system-wide exercise identifies how banks and non-banks amplify a common market shock.
milestones.criterion: Identify feedback and amplification arising from the joint responses of banks and non-bank financial institutions to a specified market shock. In the Bank of England's SWES, around 50 firms responded to a two-week hypothetical scenario. The report of 29 November 2024 found that asset sales and limited bank intermediation could amplify stress, including illiquidity in sterling corporate bonds. This fulfils a qualitative programme objective, not a forecast-accuracy standard.
milestones.set_by: Bank of England, published aims of the system-wide exploratory scenario exercise; a qualitative programme objective for UK financial markets.
milestones.threshold_quote: investigate how these behaviours and market dynamics can amplify shocks in markets and potentially pose risks to UK financial stability.

milestones.title: Banking-crisis warnings achieve relative usefulness above zero in out-of-sample evaluation.
milestones.criterion: Obtain out-of-sample relative usefulness Ur = 1 − L(μ)/min(μ,1−μ) > 0, where L(μ) weights missed-crisis and false-alarm rates by μ and 1−μ. This beats the better constant warning rule. Beutel et al. studied 15 countries and 22 crises during 1970–2016, forecasting 5–12 quarters ahead. For out-of-sample quarters from the third quarter of 2005 through the fourth quarter of 2016, their all-variable logit obtained Ur = 0.605 at μ = 0.5 (90% bootstrap interval 0.222–0.605). This tests crisis occurrence, not network propagation.
milestones.set_by: Early-warning modelling literature's relative-usefulness convention, documented and applied by Beutel, List and von Schweinitz in Appendix A.2; written for systemic banking-crisis warnings.
milestones.threshold_quote: A usefulness above (below) zero therefore means that the model is more (less) informative

milestones.title: Prospective cascade forecasts produce lower decision loss than a specified benchmark.
milestones.criterion: Forecast cascade incidence and system-wide loss using only information available when each forecast is issued, and subsequently obtain lower decision loss than a specified benchmark on events occurring after issuance. The network, horizon, cascade outcome and loss function are fixed before evaluation. Historical recursive banking-crisis forecasts and hypothetical SWES outcomes do not establish this result. No qualifying prospective cascade evaluation was located.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of BCBS, Bank of England and OFR materials and cascade-forecast benchmarks located no prospective cascade-forecast acceptance threshold.

milestones.title: A model correctly ranks a held-out intervention's causal effect on system-wide cascade losses.
milestones.criterion: Before prospective policy use, a model fitted without a held-out historical intervention correctly ranks that intervention against an alternative by system-wide cascade loss; an independently identified causal comparison confirms the ranking. Bluedorn and Park's study of the Panic of 1884 used 3,339 debtor–creditor observations from Pennsylvania during 1881–1887 and concluded that bailouts likely contained contagion. It did not validate advance model predictions of the bailout effect; it is supporting historical evidence.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of the Bank of England policy-modelling agenda and intervention-evaluation literature located no acceptance threshold for held-out predictions of cascade-prevention effects.

not_found: No published acceptance test combining prospective cascade forecasting with causally demonstrated prevention was located.
No prospective evaluation jointly establishing cascade-forecast skill and the causal benefit of model-selected interventions was located.
No independent causal evaluation validating a cascade model's intervention ranking on held-out historical evidence was located.
The publisher pages for Beutel et al. and the journal version of the Panic of 1884 study could not be opened; their supplied PDFs were accessible.
